claims.text: Pseudolaw spreads across countries, with promoters adapting US arguments to other legal systems
claims.note: A survey of 200+ Australian and NZ cases finds US sovereign-citizen pseudolaw migrated there from about 2010 and adapted to local legal discourse; US gurus ran speaking tours there in the 2010s.

claims.text: The movement grew out of the Posse Comitatus and other far-right anti-tax groups
claims.note: This law review traces the 1990s movement to four overlapping groups: Posse Comitatus, Patriot/militia groups, common-law courts and anti-tax protestors.

claims.text: Sovereign-citizen teachers profit by selling seminars, document kits and status-correction services
claims.note: Gurus are described as conmen who sell OPCA concepts for a price via seminars, books and DVDs; examples include Porisky taking about 7 percent of 800 students' income and a $500 plus 2 x $5,000 status scheme.

claims.text: Sovereign citizens are a significant source of violence against police
claims.note: Open-source compilation found 75 instances of harm or attempted harm to police, 27 officers killed (1983-July 2020) and 65 wounded; media-based and possibly incomplete.

claims.text: Sovereign citizens file false liens and nuisance filings to harass officials
claims.note: Adherents file false liens, fake letters of credit and fabricated tax reports against officials ('paper terrorism'); one couple filed $250 billion in liens against a dozen Minnesota officials.

claims.text: Sovereign-citizen beliefs spread most during hardship such as foreclosure crises and pandemics
claims.note: Recruitment surges are documented around the 1980s farm crisis, 2008 foreclosures and COVID, though growth also tracks the internet and other factors.

claims.text: Common law, the Magna Carta or natural law override statutes for a free person who rejects them
claims.note: All but three provisions of Magna Carta were repealed by 1969, and the High Court of Australia held in 1905 that invalidity for nonconformity with Magna Carta is 'not one for serious refutation'; McHugh J called it political ideals that do not bind parliaments.

claims.text: Courts uniformly reject sovereign-citizen arguments as frivolous
claims.note: In 1089 Canadian OPCA decisions the litigation was invariably unsuccessful, and all 51 OPCA-linked Supreme Court leave applications were refused; no court anywhere has endorsed the memeplex.

claims.text: The government creates a separate corporate entity, the strawman, in your all-caps name
claims.note: The strawman concept 'has no basis in law in either the US or Canada -- it is simply a myth', and courts have said so time and again.

claims.text: Moorish Americans are a sovereign people exempt from US law under a treaty with Morocco
claims.note: Seventh Circuit (Posner): the claim that eighteenth-century treaties put Moors outside US jurisdiction and taxation has no basis in fact; a self-described Moor is a US citizen with no immunity from US law, and the suit was frivolous.

claims.text: The United States became a private corporation under the District of Columbia Act of 1871
claims.note: The Supreme Court describes the 1871 Act as making the District of Columbia 'a body corporate for municipal purposes', a mere municipal corporation; sovereign power over the District stays with the US government and Congress.

claims.text: Sovereign citizens use fake deeds to take over homes they do not own
claims.note: Numerous prosecutions involve sovereign or Moorish adherents filing bogus deeds and squatting in vacant or listed homes.

claims.text: Courts have no jurisdiction over you unless you consent or contract with them
claims.note: The Seventh Circuit holds that whatever status a person claims (sovereign citizen, secured-party creditor, flesh-and-blood human), that person is not beyond the courts' jurisdiction; the defendants' insistence that they did not consent changed nothing and they were tried and convicted.

claims.text: A gold-fringed flag means a courtroom is operating under admiralty or maritime law
claims.note: The court reviews flag law: fringe is not part of the flag, has no heraldic or legal significance, and cannot change a court's jurisdiction, which 'is a matter of law, statute, and constitution'. It cites several courts calling the argument frivolous.

claims.text: A constitutional right to travel means a private person needs no driver's license to drive a private car
claims.note: The Supreme Court upheld conviction of a man driving his own car from his office into Maryland without the required registration; licensing private drivers is valid police power.

claims.text: Sovereign-citizen defendants usually end up worse off than if they had argued normally
claims.note: Author (court litigant-management counsel) says OPCA litigation is often self-destructive, endorsing the quip that it turns a $50 traffic ticket into jail as 'the truth'.

claims.text: Defendants who win while using sovereign-citizen arguments win on ordinary legal grounds, not on the theory
claims.note: The guru acquittals cited were on ordinary grounds: Porisky because the Crown had not proved its non-filing records, Naudi because the Crown had not linked him to his SIN.

claims.text: A birth certificate is a bond or security traded to fund a secret account in your name
claims.note: Treasury says a birth certificate has no monetary value, cannot be used for purchases or to claim bonds, and the 'Exemption Account' is fictitious and does not exist in the Treasury system.

claims.text: Tax refunds claimed through sovereign-citizen trust filings are fraudulent and get clawed back
claims.note: Trust 'untaxing' and SSN-card trust filings are frivolous and draw civil and criminal penalties (Lizalek: trust held nonexistent, income taxed, penalties); the document does not show refunds actually paid and later recovered.

claims.text: Sovereign-citizen filings can extract real refunds when tax agencies fail to verify claimed payments
claims.note: Documented CRA and IRS cases show bogus returns paid out because withholding claims were not checked before refunds were issued.

claims.text: An apparent win reinforces a sovereign citizen's belief that the theory works
claims.note: Researchers of conspiracy belief describe intermittent apparent successes as strongly reinforcing, though measured evidence is mostly qualitative.

claims.text: Birth certificates carry CUSIP numbers that show they are registered securities
claims.note: CUSIPs identify registered securities; numbers on birth certificates are state file numbers, and no birth-certificate securities exist.

claims.text: All-caps names on legal documents are a typographic convention with no legal effect
claims.note: Courts and style manuals treat capitalisation as formatting; judges routinely hold it has no legal significance.

claims.text: Business entities like an LLC separate personal liability from business debts
claims.note: LLCs and corporations do limit owner liability, but personal guarantees, veil-piercing and personal torts often reach the owner.

claims.text: You can draw on a secret Treasury account to pay debts by writing "accepted for value" on bills
claims.note: Citing the 6th Circuit (Anderson), the Treasury does not maintain depository accounts against which an individual can draw; secret per-citizen accounts are 'pure fantasy' and fictitious instruments can be prosecuted under 18 USC 514.

claims.text: Since the 1933 gold suspension, money is credit and debts cannot be lawfully paid, only discharged
claims.note: HJR 192 declares US currency legal tender for all debts and measures obligations in dollars; the court says it addresses only the move off gold and supports no theory of discharge rather than payment.

claims.text: The US federal government is a private corporation rather than a lawful sovereign government
claims.note: A district court held the United States is a sovereign, not a corporation, and called contrary arguments wholly frivolous; the Tax Court sanctioned a taxpayer arguing 'the United States is a corporation'; trial-level rulings.

claims.text: Filing a UCC-1 financing statement gives you ownership and control of your strawman
claims.note: Filing UCC-1 statements with birth certificates to 'redeem' the straw man is a frivolous redemption theory that courts call implausible and clearly nonsense.

claims.text: Statutes are contracts or corporate policy that bind only people who consent to them
claims.note: A freeman who said he never consented to NZ's Land Transport Act had his appeal struck out as an abuse of process; Shaw v AG (WA) held a Constitution Act is a statute, not a contract.

claims.text: Using a car for private travel rather than commerce is not driving under the motor vehicle laws
claims.note: A driver with a homemade 'private' plate who claimed a right to travel privately without a license was convicted of license and plate offenses, affirmed on appeal.

claims.text: In many states a driver stopped by police must produce a license, but a passenger need not identify themselves
claims.note: Drivers must show a licence and passengers generally need not identify absent reasonable suspicion, but stop-and-identify laws and officer-safety orders vary by state.

claims.text: Declaring yourself an American State National removes you from federal and state statutory jurisdiction
claims.note: Circuits rejected claims that being a citizen of a state or 'state republic' rather than the US puts one beyond federal court jurisdiction (2d Cir. Drachenberg, 7th Cir. Hilgeford); federal tax context only, so state jurisdiction is not covered.

claims.text: State national paperwork or passports protect the holder from being detained by police
claims.note: US passports confer no immunity; state-national documents carry no legal weight and holders are arrested like anyone else.

claims.text: Federal income tax paid to the IRS goes to a foreign corporation rather than the US Treasury
claims.note: The IRS is organised under the Secretary of the Treasury to administer the internal revenue laws, not a private or foreign corporation; the document does not trace where receipts are deposited.

claims.text: Millions of Americans have formally changed their status to American State National
claims.note: There is no legal status change to record; the figure is unsourced and no government recognises such corrections.

claims.text: Sovereign-citizen debt-discharge instruments are worthless and using them can be prosecuted as fraud
claims.note: 1099-OIDs, bonded promissory notes and Treasury 'checks' are not payment of any debt; circuits upheld convictions for passing fictitious instruments (6th Cir. Heath, 8th Cir. Getzschman, 8th Cir. Johnson).

claims.text: People who stop filing taxes on sovereign-citizen grounds face penalties and prosecution
claims.note: Filing is mandatory under IRC 6012; non-filers face civil and criminal penalties, and circuits upheld failure-to-file convictions of people arguing filing is voluntary; the document covers tax-protester grounds generally, including sovereign/state-citizen arguments.

claims.text: Sovereign-citizen ideas spread through prisons and jails
claims.note: The FBI and Bureau of Prisons have documented redemption and sovereign teachings circulating among inmates.

claims.text: The IRS formally lists sovereign-citizen arguments as frivolous tax positions
claims.note: The IRS publishes a list of frivolous positions (Notice 2010-33) that includes the claim of being a state citizen not subject to federal tax, and warns of penalties for it in revenue rulings.

claims.text: Promoters blame failed filings on the user's procedural mistakes rather than the theory
claims.note: Court opinions and researchers describe gurus attributing failures to user error and selling updated materials.

claims.text: UCC filing offices record filings without checking validity, so acceptance proves nothing
claims.note: Under the UCC as enacted in California, filing offices have little authority to refuse fraudulent filings and do not judge validity; false, deficient liens are routinely accepted and the named debtor must prove them false.

claims.text: The sovereign-citizen movement's founders came from the racist Christian Identity movement
claims.note: The review says Posse Comitatus, the first root of the movement, was a radical right-wing Christian Identity sect tied to white supremacist Christian Identity.

claims.text: Americans are misidentified at birth as federal citizens through deceptive hospital paperwork
claims.note: Under the Fourteenth Amendment persons born in the US and subject to its jurisdiction are citizens at birth by operation of law, not by hospital paperwork.

claims.text: Recording expatriation and name declarations at a land records office legally changes your political status
claims.note: Recorders accept documents without validating them; citizenship status changes only through federal renunciation procedures.

claims.text: Reclaiming state national status restores your rights and control over your property
claims.note: The paperwork has no legal effect on rights or property; courts ignore it.

claims.text: The Moorish Science Temple disavows the sovereign-citizen claims made in its name
claims.note: The MSTA home office stated it is neither a sovereign-citizen nor a tax-protester movement, and a Georgia temple called sovereign-citizen propaganda 'completely asinine'.

claims.text: A notary stamp only verifies a signature and gives a document no extra legal force
claims.note: Notarization authenticates the signer's identity and signature; it does not validate the document's contents.

claims.text: Adherents called themselves sovereign citizens before disowning the label as an oxymoron
claims.note: 1990s seminars and books by movement figures used 'sovereign citizen' as a self-description before it became pejorative.

claims.text: State jural assemblies of state nationals hold lawful judicial authority
claims.note: These assemblies have no legal standing; their 'courts' and rulings are unrecognised and members have been prosecuted for acting on them.

claims.text: Juries can throw out any law they find unjust through jury nullification
claims.note: Criminal juries can acquit against the evidence, but that sets no precedent and does not void any law, and judges may remove jurors who announce it.

claims.text: Reconstruction never ended and the US remains under a foreign military government
claims.note: Reconstruction ended in 1877 and civilian constitutional government has operated since; the claim has no documentary basis.

claims.text: Courts consistently uphold driver licensing and registration as a valid exercise of state police power
claims.note: US Supreme Court: a state may require registration of motor vehicles and licensing of drivers with reasonable fees as an exercise of the police power, including for interstate travellers.

claims.text: Refusing to show a license or identify yourself at a traffic stop gets you released rather than arrested
claims.note: A driver who refused license, registration and name was removed from the car, arrested and convicted of obstruction, failure to disclose and failure to display; one case.

claims.text: Sovereign-citizen arguments at traffic stops commonly escalate into arrest, towing and extra charges
claims.note: Widely documented stops end with broken windows, arrest, impound and obstruction or resisting charges, though some end with a ticket.

claims.text: Police may lawfully order a driver out of the car during a traffic stop
claims.note: Pennsylvania v. Mimms (1977) lets officers order drivers out during a lawful stop.

claims.text: Courts have ruled that a license is not required to travel by automobile
claims.note: The court cites its own and other courts' repeated rejection of right-to-travel-without-a-license arguments. The rulings run the other way.

claims.text: The right-to-travel case Thompson v. Smith concerned arbitrary license revocation, not a right to drive unlicensed
claims.note: The 1930 Virginia decision struck an arbitrary revocation ordinance while affirming the city's power to license drivers.

claims.text: Renouncing US citizenship or claiming state national status exempts you from federal income tax
claims.note: Claims to be solely a citizen of a sovereign state and not subject to federal tax are uniformly rejected (14th Amendment gives simultaneous state and federal citizenship); the document does not address formal expatriation, so this judges the state-national prong.

claims.text: Court orders without a wet-ink signature or court seal are void
claims.note: Courts issue valid orders electronically and without seals; judges uniformly reject the wet-ink argument.

claims.text: Signing a contract "all rights reserved UCC 1-308" keeps you from being bound as the debtor
claims.note: 1-308 only keeps rights a party reserves while it performs or assents to performance; it is about continuing performance despite a dispute, not escaping the obligation as debtor.

claims.text: Your signature creates the credit a lender extends, making you the true creditor
claims.note: The claim that the borrower creates the loaned money by signature is called erroneous; the one supporting case (Credit River, 1968) was declared a nullity and rejected in Commonwealth courts.

claims.text: A lender's failure to explain how your signature creates credit is fraud that voids the debt
claims.note: Truth in Lending requires disclosure of credit terms, not this theory; courts dismiss nondisclosure-of-credit-creation claims.

claims.text: Under federal law you can dispute a debt collector's claim within 30 days and demand verification
claims.note: The FDCPA gives a 30-day validation right against third-party collectors, but not against original creditors and not to a 'full accounting'.

claims.text: Signing with "UCC 1-308" or "without prejudice" stops a court from binding you to the law
claims.note: UCC 1-308's text and official comment: it lets a party keep performing a commercial contract under protest during a dispute without waiving reserved rights. It says nothing about courts or criminal law.

claims.text: A traffic ticket is an offer to contract that you can refuse
claims.note: In Ohio the uniform traffic ticket serves as the complaint and summons, a charging document rather than an offer to contract.

claims.text: Challenging a court's jurisdiction and demanding proof of a contract gets traffic tickets dismissed
claims.note: The defendant's notice to abate, sovereignty affidavit and jurisdiction challenge were summarily overruled and he was convicted on all traffic and related charges; one case.

claims.text: Magna Carta Article 61 gives people a lawful right to refuse laws they deem invalid
claims.note: Clause 61 was annulled within months in 1215 and never reissued; UK courts reject 'lawful rebellion' defences.

claims.text: Writing "UCC 1-308 refused" on a ticket and returning it within three days voids it
claims.note: The section covers performance under reservation of rights in commercial dealings; it contains no time limit and no mechanism for voiding citations.

claims.text: Any contract can be cancelled during a legally guaranteed three- or seven-day cooling-off period
claims.note: Cooling-off rights exist only for specific transactions such as door-to-door sales or some loans, not contracts in general.

claims.text: Sovereign-citizen gurus are frequently convicted of fraud for the schemes they sell
claims.note: Many promoters of untaxing and pseudolegal tax schemes were convicted (Meredith 121 months, Ambort 108 months, Schiff 12+ years, eight trust promoters in Scott); this is a case list, not a rate.

claims.text: The sovereign-citizen movement has grown since 2020 by recruiting from QAnon, MAGA and anti-vaccine audiences
claims.note: Monitoring groups documented heavy crossover since 2020, though membership counts are estimates.

claims.text: Sovereign citizens create fake courts, governments and law enforcement bodies with no legal authority
claims.note: Groups set up vigilante police ('Territorial Marshals', C3POs) and 'Tacit Supreme in Law' courts claiming jurisdiction superior to the government's.

claims.text: Writing a phrase such as "under duress" next to a signature voids the legal obligation
claims.note: Duress is a factual defence that must be proven; a notation on a signature does not create it.

claims.text: Declaring yourself a living man rather than a legal person places you outside the jurisdiction of the law
claims.note: Appellate court: a 'flesh-and-blood human being' or 'sovereign citizen' is not beyond the courts' jurisdiction, and such theories 'should be rejected summarily, however they are presented'.

claims.text: Filing a UCC-1 financing statement on your strawman name releases you from its debts and obligations
claims.note: The plaintiff filed UCC-1/UCC-3 statements naming herself as secured party over her all-caps 'fictitious entity', yet her mortgage debt was not discharged and her claims were dismissed with prejudice.

claims.text: Filing a Form 1099-OID lets you claim money back from the Treasury
claims.note: Form 1099-OID only reports interest income; it is not a financial instrument or a way to withdraw money from the Treasury, and the 8th Circuit upheld convictions for 1099-OID refund schemes.

claims.text: Redemption paperwork lets people erase all their personal debts
claims.note: Redemption instruments (1099-OID, bonded notes, sight drafts on a Treasury account) are no legitimate method of paying any public or private debt, and using them risks criminal charges.

claims.text: Officers who detain a state national face large personal fines payable to the detainee
claims.note: No law sets such fines; self-styled fee schedules are unenforceable and suits on them are dismissed.

claims.text: The 14th Amendment made Americans corporate persons or property of the federal government
claims.note: The amendment conferred citizenship and equal protection; it created no corporate status or second-class citizen.

claims.text: The sovereign-citizen movement is fragmented among competing gurus with conflicting theories
claims.note: The Canadian OPCA community is 'highly fragmented', with many gurus competing for a shrinking, skeptical customer base.

claims.text: A land patent gives an owner allodial title that protects the property from taxes and foreclosure
claims.note: The Seventh Circuit called a self-drafted 'land patent' recorded to defeat a mortgage a blatant attempt to improve title by personal fiat; it did not improve title, foreclosure stood, and the court imposed sanctions for a frivolous appeal.

claims.text: A county recorder who refuses sovereign filings can be claimed against personally through their surety bond
claims.note: Official bonds cover real misconduct; refusing bogus filings is lawful and such bond claims fail.

claims.text: The Seventh Amendment guarantees a jury trial in any dispute over twenty dollars
claims.note: It applies to federal civil suits at common law, not to state courts, equity or administrative matters.

claims.text: A mortgage is void because the bank created the loan money from nothing
claims.note: 'Banks loan nothing of value because they create money from thin air' is erroneous; Credit River, which denied a bank recovery on that basis, was declared a nullity and rejected in Australian and Canadian courts.

claims.text: Persistent pseudolegal administrative filings get creditors to drop claims or offer favorable settlements
claims.note: Only sellers' anecdotes support it; creditors usually proceed and courts disregard such records.

claims.text: Federal consumer laws such as the FDCPA give debtors real remedies against abusive collectors
claims.note: The FDCPA and FCRA provide debt validation rights and statutory damages, though awards are usually modest.

claims.text: Closed bank accounts can be used to pay debts by electronic transfer or setoff
claims.note: Payments drawn on closed accounts bounce and are reversed; knowingly using them is fraud.

claims.text: The Constitution was never validly ratified and the Articles of Confederation still govern
claims.note: The Constitution was ratified in 1788 and replaced the Articles; every court applies it.

claims.text: Pseudolegal payments to creditors may post at first but are later reversed, leaving the debt plus fees
claims.note: Billing systems can post an item before it clears; bogus drafts are then returned and late fees apply.

claims.text: The Federal Reserve holds accounts only for banks and institutions, not individual citizens
claims.note: Federal Reserve Banks offer accounts to depository institutions and some government bodies, not to individuals.

claims.text: The UCC rights-reservation section was renumbered from 1-207 to 1-308 to stop people using it
claims.note: The section was indeed formerly 1-207, but the official comment says it is 'identical to former Section 1-207', so the renumbering changed nothing and gives no sign of an aim to stop its use.

claims.text: Admiralty cases in the US are heard by ordinary federal district courts, not separate admiralty courts
claims.note: 28 U.S.C. 1333 gives admiralty jurisdiction to the federal district courts.

claims.text: Sovereign-citizen testimonials of courtroom wins are false or cite decisions that do not exist
claims.note: Researchers who check claimed wins find none on the theory; apparent wins are dismissals on ordinary grounds or unverifiable.

claims.text: Driver licensing and registration exist mainly to extract money for the DMV and insurers
claims.note: The Court found the purpose was public safety and order plus compensation for costly roads, and held the statute 'is not a mere revenue measure'.

claims.text: Sovereign citizens misread court opinions by quoting recited facts or arguments as if they were the ruling
claims.note: Judges and researchers note pseudolaw promoters routinely cite case passages out of context or from party arguments.

claims.text: Lenders and title companies refuse loan documents signed with UCC 1-308 reservations
claims.note: Lenders require clean signatures for funding and routinely reject annotated documents, though evidence is mostly anecdotal.

claims.text: Pseudolegal loopholes let homeowners walk away from mortgage obligations
claims.note: Because the bill of exchange was not valid payment, the lender 'was within [its] rights to foreclose'; all claims were dismissed with prejudice.

claims.text: Registering a car, property or child signs ownership over to the government
claims.note: Registration records ownership or a birth; it does not transfer title to the state.

claims.text: Serving a notice of claim of right on the government gives lawful excuse to disobey statutes
claims.note: The Freeman 'Notice of Understanding, Intent, and Claim of Right' is meant to withdraw consent, but unilateral rejection of state authority was refused leave as having no legal merit.

claims.text: A borrower owes a bank nothing unless the bank can prove it suffered a loss on the loan
claims.note: A loan contract obliges repayment whether or not the lender sold the note; vapour-money arguments are uniformly rejected.

claims.text: Ordinary wages are not taxable income under federal law
claims.note: IRC 61 defines gross income to include compensation for services, and appellate courts (e.g. 3d Cir. Connor: every court has unequivocally rejected the argument that wages are not income) sanction the contrary argument.

claims.text: Giving up a social insurance or social security number frees a person from income tax
claims.note: Tax liability depends on income and residence, not on holding an identifying number.

claims.text: Sovereign-citizen beliefs are sustained by online groups that reinforce each other's legal theories
claims.note: Occupants of the OPCAsphere reinforce each other's beliefs by circulating documents, videos and memes; psychologists found the beliefs reinforced in OPCA communities.

claims.text: Paying income tax is voluntary
claims.note: IRC 1 imposes the tax and 6151 requires payment; 'voluntary' in Flora refers to self-assessment, and multiple circuits (8th Drefke, 9th Wilcox, 2d Banat) reject the voluntary-payment argument as frivolous with sanctions.

claims.text: Self-convened common-law courts have real legal authority to try and sentence officials
claims.note: Such bodies have no legal standing; their verdicts are unenforceable and acting on them can itself be a crime.

claims.text: Sovereign-citizen adherents increasingly reject the label while keeping the same beliefs
claims.note: Researchers and police report rebranding as living men, state nationals or common-law groups with unchanged doctrine.

claims.text: A lost Titles of Nobility 13th Amendment strips lawyers and judges of citizenship and voids the courts
claims.note: The Titles of Nobility Amendment was never ratified, and courts reject the argument.

claims.text: Holding sovereign-citizen beliefs is legal; only crimes committed on their behalf are prosecutable
claims.note: In the US belief and speech are protected; investigation needs a crime, and the FBI requires force or violence for domestic terrorism.

claims.text: Citizen-convened common-law grand juries have legal authority to check government
claims.note: Only grand juries summoned by courts under statute have legal power; self-convened ones have none.

claims.text: The Supreme Court has described the grand jury as belonging to no branch of government
claims.note: United States v. Williams (1992) says this, but of court-summoned grand juries, not self-convened ones.

claims.text: A person can ignore a licensing law that restricts a constitutional right and act with impunity
claims.note: Licensing does not unlawfully restrict the right to travel; the defendant who ignored it was convicted and the convictions were affirmed.

claims.text: Traffic infractions are not crimes
claims.note: Many states classify minor traffic violations as civil infractions, but driving unlicensed or unregistered is often a misdemeanor.

claims.text: The Constitution protects a fundamental right to travel freely between states
claims.note: The Court recognizes, per Crandall v. Nevada, a right of US citizens to pass through the states that a direct exit tax would violate, while upholding licensing.

claims.text: Courts bar repeat pseudolaw litigants with civil restraint or vexatious-litigant orders
claims.note: Alberta's 2013 OPCA Master Order blocked filings and a persistent Freeman was declared a vexatious litigant needing leave to file; the early screen ended 95% of attempts to start OPCA litigation.

claims.text: A struggling borrower does better negotiating a repayment plan with the lender than using pseudolaw
claims.note: Courts accept realistic arrears plans while pseudolaw defences fail and add costs.

claims.text: The original US Constitution was replaced in 1871 by a separate corporate constitution
claims.note: The 1871 Act only set up a municipal government for the District, with powers 'not inconsistent with the constitution and laws of the United States'. It replaced no constitution and was itself abolished in 1874.

claims.text: The United States remains a colony of the British Crown or the Vatican
claims.note: Britain recognised US independence in the 1783 Treaty of Paris; no legal authority supports continuing Crown or Vatican control.

claims.text: House Joint Resolution 192 was a legal-tender law that let debts be paid in dollars instead of gold
claims.note: HJR 192 made gold-payment clauses against public policy and US currency legal tender for all debts; the Supreme Court read it as tying obligations to the number of dollars promised.

claims.text: A state must give due process before suspending a driver's license
claims.note: Bell v. Burson requires procedural due process to suspend a license but does not bar requiring one.

claims.text: Frivolous pseudolegal tax filings draw civil penalties
claims.note: Frivolous returns draw accuracy, civil-fraud and erroneous-refund penalties plus a $5,000 IRC 6702 penalty for positions on the IRS's published frivolous list; the document lists many cases imposing them.

claims.text: The US government went bankrupt in 1933 and pledged citizens as collateral
claims.note: Treasury describes the story that the government 'somehow went bankrupt' in 1933 and traded citizens' birth certificates, and calls the theory 'bogus and incomprehensible'.

claims.text: Arguing the right to travel in traffic court gets no-plates tickets dismissed
claims.note: The right-to-travel defendant was convicted of failure to display a license plate, and the appeal court affirmed; one case.

claims.text: Only a few clauses of Magna Carta remain in force in UK law
claims.note: By 1969 the whole Charter, save three provisions, had been repealed in England.

claims.text: Formally renouncing citizenship is the only lawful way to opt out of a state's authority
claims.note: Renunciation is lawful and ends citizenship, but not the authority of the country you live in, and tax obligations may remain.

claims.text: Taxation of individuals is illegal
claims.note: The 16th Amendment authorizes a non-apportioned income tax on US citizens; the Supreme Court upheld it in Brushaber and courts have consistently rejected challenges.

claims.text: The ink colour used to sign a document changes its legal effect
claims.note: No law gives signature ink colour any legal meaning.

claims.text: Suing police over a right-to-travel arrest wins large damage awards
claims.note: Section 1983 suits on right-to-travel theories are dismissed as frivolous, for example Ford v. Anones.

claims.text: An officer who makes a traffic stop with emergency lights for a non-emergency commits a felony
claims.note: Police may use lights to make lawful traffic stops; no statute makes that a felony.

claims.text: Drivers can lawfully decline to answer an officer's questions at a traffic stop
claims.note: The right to silence covers questions, but drivers must still produce license and registration and in many states identify themselves.

claims.text: Becoming a citizen forfeits all your property and labour to the state
claims.note: Citizenship statutes confer status; they transfer no property, and citizens own property in their own names under ordinary law.

claims.text: Income tax is a franchise fee owed only by people who accept state-created legal personhood
claims.note: The 10th Circuit upheld penalties for arguing that the income tax is an excise on privileged activities, and IRC 1 taxes individuals' income regardless of claimed status.

claims.text: Tax authorities back off people who refuse to pay on sovereign grounds rather than risk a public court loss
claims.note: Most charged protesters are convicted, and even after an acquittal the IRS may still pursue the underlying tax and civil penalties; the document lists many pursued cases.

claims.text: Telling a court you are not the legal person named in the charges makes prosecutors drop them
claims.note: Defendants who said they were a living man and not the named person all lost; the court found them identifiable by the legal name.

claims.text: Equity and trust filings can recover your property from a public trust the state holds it in
claims.note: No public trust holds citizens' property; pseudolegal trust filings have no effect and courts dismiss them.

claims.text: Sovereign-citizen belief is driven by a desire for control and status more than by legal argument
claims.note: Pseudolaw lets adherents disregard legal norms and disempower state actors while still seeing themselves as lawful, which fits a control motive but is not measured.

claims.text: Many people drawn into pseudolaw come through family court, child-protection or protection-order disputes
claims.note: Commentators and Meads v Meads note family-law litigants are common among pseudolaw users, but no measured share exists.

claims.text: Sending police or officials a fee schedule creates a debt they must pay
claims.note: Unilateral fee schedules create no contract; no court has enforced one and some senders have been prosecuted.

claims.text: Lawyers refuse to argue sovereign-citizen theories because their duty to the court forbids baseless arguments
claims.note: Professional conduct rules bar advancing frivolous arguments, which is why most pseudolaw litigants are self-represented.

claims.text: Courts follow Meads v Meads in dismissing pseudolegal arguments summarily without rebutting each one
claims.note: Meads has been cited in 198 Canadian decisions, endorsed by five Courts of Appeal and followed across the Commonwealth, sparing judges from answering arguments 'piecemeal'; but only 33.6% of later OPCA judgments cite it.

claims.text: A person may lawfully resist an unlawful arrest
claims.note: Canadian and some US law recognise it in principle, but many US states have abolished the right and resisting is dangerous and rarely vindicated.

claims.text: Giving police your name or information creates a contract with them
claims.note: Identifying yourself to police forms no contract; police authority comes from statute, not agreement.

claims.text: Most money in a modern economy is created by commercial banks when they make loans
claims.note: The Bank of England's 2014 bulletin and standard monetary economics describe bank lending creating deposits.

claims.text: The government pledged its citizens and their property as collateral for its debts to bankers
claims.note: The court sets out the theory that citizens are pledged as security for the national debt and rejects it as revisionist history and conspiracy theory; the authorities cited only concern leaving the gold standard.

claims.text: Congress pledged the United States to foreign bankers in 1871 to cover Civil War debts
claims.note: No 1871 statute or record shows such a pledge; Civil War debt was financed by public bonds.

claims.text: Constitutional amendments ratified after 1871, including the income tax amendment, are void
claims.note: The 16th Amendment was ratified by 40+ states and certified in 1913; courts hold the certification conclusive and reject non-ratification claims, so the income tax amendment is valid (only that amendment is covered).

claims.text: Writing a name in all capitals in a legal document marks it as a corporation
claims.note: The Tax Court (Holmes) dismissed as frivolous the claim that IRS letters addressed in all capitals treat the taxpayer as a fictional corporate entity, and imposed a $10,000 penalty.

claims.text: Income tax was illegal under the original Constitution
claims.note: The original Constitution allowed income taxes if apportioned and the Civil War income tax was upheld; the 16th Amendment removed apportionment.

claims.text: Signing a mortgage or opening a bank account signs away your rights through a power of attorney
claims.note: Mortgages and account agreements are ordinary contracts with defined terms; they grant no general power of attorney.

claims.text: The Federal Reserve is a private corporation that owns the currency it issues
claims.note: Regional reserve banks have member-bank stockholders, but the Fed is a government-created system and its notes are obligations of the United States.

claims.text: The IRS is a private corporation chartered in Delaware, not part of the Treasury
claims.note: The IRS is an agency created under the Treasury Secretary's IRC 7801 authority with a Commissioner under 7803; the 11th Circuit held it is clearly an agency of the United States and courts call the private-corporation claim wholly frivolous.

claims.text: The president has ruled under continuous unconstitutional emergency powers since 1933
claims.note: The 1976 National Emergencies Act ended the old emergencies; current emergencies are specific, statutory and reviewable.

claims.text: Hiring a lawyer automatically gives the court jurisdiction over you
claims.note: The court cites precedent that federal courts have subject-matter and personal jurisdiction over defendants brought before them on federal indictments; jurisdiction comes from the indictment and law, not from hiring counsel.

claims.text: Bracketing contract terms you disagree with removes them from the contract
claims.note: Unilateral marks do not alter a contract unless the other party agrees; style manuals have no legal effect.

claims.text: The tax code's definition of person means the law treats you as a corporation
claims.note: The tax code's 'person' expressly includes an individual alongside corporations, so being a 'person' does not make one a corporation; courts reject the not-a-person argument.

claims.text: US citizens under the Fourteenth Amendment have no access to the Bill of Rights
claims.note: Courts apply the Bill of Rights to all citizens, and the 14th Amendment incorporated most of it against the states.

claims.text: The Fourteenth Amendment was never lawfully ratified
claims.note: The 14th Amendment was certified in 1868 and courts have rejected challenges to its ratification.

claims.text: An unrebutted notarized affidavit is the highest truth in law and binds the agency that receives it
claims.note: The court found no authority that maxims like 'an unrebutted affidavit stands as truth in commerce' have binding force, and held that non-response created no estoppel.

claims.text: Legislators have no authority to regulate the behaviour of the people
claims.note: The Constitution grants legislative power and states have broad police power to regulate conduct.

claims.text: Speeding laws apply only to commercial drivers, not private travellers
claims.note: Speed limits apply to every driver on public roads; courts reject the commercial-only reading.

claims.text: Traffic cases against private travellers are dismissed for lack of jurisdiction when commerce is not proven
claims.note: The state argued the driver was not in commerce at all, and his conviction was affirmed; state motor vehicle rules reach all vehicles on its highways, so no commerce needs to be proved.

claims.text: A warranty deed is only colour of title and gives no real ownership
claims.note: A warranty deed conveys full legal title from the grantor; the original patent passes with the chain of title automatically.

claims.text: A properly secured land patent has never lost in an appellate court
claims.note: Appellate courts repeatedly reject land-patent defences to taxes and foreclosure, e.g. Hilgeford v. Peoples Bank.

claims.text: Without re-securing the land patent, a prior claimant can evict you from land you bought
claims.note: Title passes through recorded deeds; a patent cannot be reclaimed by a prior owner to evict a later buyer.

claims.text: A state cannot charge a licence fee for exercising a constitutional right, so licensing private travel is unconstitutional
claims.note: The Supreme Court upheld registration and operator license fees graduated by horsepower as a valid police-power measure and fair compensation for roads, not a violation of the right to pass through the state.

claims.text: The FBI classifies the sovereign-citizen movement as domestic terrorism
claims.note: The FBI's own Law Enforcement Bulletin states the FBI considers sovereign-citizen extremists a domestic terrorist movement (the label attaches to the extremists, not every believer).

claims.text: Gold fringe on a US flag signals that martial law is in effect
claims.note: No law requires or forbids fringe; per the Army Adjutant General and Attorney General it is 'without heraldic significance', and fringe does not turn a flag into a flag of war.

claims.text: The US sovereign-citizen movement numbers in the hundreds of thousands
claims.note: SPLC estimates around 300,000, but there is no membership and figures are rough guesses.

claims.text: Citizens are creditors of the government and can use the debt it owes them to discharge their own debts
claims.note: The claim that a person can use the government's supposed debt to her to discharge debts to third parties by a bill of exchange was rejected; the tender was worthless and the foreclosure was lawful.

claims.text: The government creates large sums of money against each person's Social Security number
claims.note: Treasury: there is no monetary value to a birth certificate or social security number, and TreasuryDirect accounts only hold what the owner funds from their own bank account.

claims.text: Owning land in fee simple or allodium exempts it from property tax
claims.note: Fee simple land is taxed everywhere in the US and courts and attorneys general reject allodial-title tax exemptions.

claims.text: A driver lawfully stopped by police must produce a license when asked
claims.note: Ohio statute: an operator shall display the driver's license on demand of a peace officer and shall not refuse; this is one state's law, applied on appeal.

claims.text: Sovereign citizens follow shared scripts and jargon for police encounters
claims.note: Researchers and police training material document widely shared scripts, phrases and document templates.

claims.text: Constitutional rights such as travel are subject to reasonable regulation like licensing
claims.note: The Supreme Court held that reasonable motor vehicle licensing and fees do not infringe citizens' right to pass through a state; the law merely regulates dangerous machines and charges for road use.

claims.text: Immigration checkpoints near the border may stop vehicles and ask about citizenship without suspicion
claims.note: United States v. Martinez-Fuerte upheld suspicionless stops and brief questioning at fixed checkpoints.

claims.text: The Uniform Commercial Code is the source of motor vehicle licensing law
claims.note: Maryland had a full motor vehicle licensing and registration statute in 1910, upheld in 1915 as police power, decades before the UCC existed.

claims.text: The constitutional right to travel protects moving between states, not operating a vehicle
claims.note: Ohio holds the travel right does not cover driving a car, but also recognizes a fundamental right of intrastate travel, so the 'between states' limit is too narrow.

claims.text: In stop-and-identify states, refusing to give your name during a lawful stop can itself be a crime
claims.note: Ohio R.C. 2921.29 makes it an offense to refuse name, address or date of birth to an officer with reasonable suspicion; the driver was convicted of it.

claims.text: To rely on the right to silence with police you must invoke it explicitly
claims.note: Berghuis v. Thompkins held that a suspect must unambiguously invoke the right to remain silent.

claims.text: A driver can refuse consent to a vehicle search, and the refusal alone cannot justify a search
claims.note: Consent must be voluntary and courts hold refusal cannot by itself supply probable cause, though other exceptions may still allow a search.

claims.text: Documenting a stop and suing under Section 1983 gets compensation for police rights violations
claims.note: Section 1983 is the real remedy, but qualified immunity and litigation costs mean most claims do not pay out.

claims.text: Writing your name in lowercase or with special punctuation changes your legal status
claims.note: Litigants styled as 'scott-william of the house of Larsen' or 'S-I-R-Crown' were unsuccessful; the legal name still identified them.

claims.text: A homestead declaration does not stop foreclosure for unpaid property taxes
claims.note: Homestead protections shield against personal creditors, and most states let counties foreclose for property tax regardless.

claims.text: Federal law applies only in the District of Columbia, federal territories and enclaves
claims.note: Courts uniformly reject the argument that the US consists only of DC, territories and enclaves; 7th, 6th, 9th and 11th Circuits called it frivolous and the 16th Amendment tax applies nationwide.

claims.text: Surrendering your driver's license and having no ID on file leaves police unable to prosecute you
claims.note: Police can detain and book unidentified people and prosecute under fingerprints or a John Doe name; refusing ID usually adds charges.

claims.text: A company's refusal to accept a UCC 1-308 signature proves the reservation has legal force
claims.note: A company declining altered contract terms shows only caution about its arbitration clause, not that the notation exempts anyone from law.

claims.text: A contract is not legally binding unless both parties understand and agree to every term
claims.note: Courts enforce signed standard-form contracts whether or not the signer read or understood every term.

claims.text: Moorish sovereign citizens blend sovereign-citizen ideas with Moorish Science Temple beliefs
claims.note: The court says sovereign-citizen ideas appeal to many self-described Moors, who combine them with Noble Drew Ali's teachings (treaty claims, strawman names), though the Temple itself rejects them.

claims.text: Handing your driver's license to an officer consents to being treated as a commercial driver
claims.note: Ordinary licenses are non-commercial and showing one creates no commercial status or contract.

claims.text: Federal motor-carrier rules that exempt private drivers show state traffic laws reach only commercial drivers
claims.note: FMCSA rules govern interstate carriers only; state traffic codes separately cover all drivers, and courts reject reading one through the other.

claims.text: All driver's licenses are commercial licenses
claims.note: States issue distinct non-commercial and commercial (CDL) licenses; an ordinary license confers no commercial status.

claims.text: Traffic cases are civil administrative matters that fail unless the state first holds an agency hearing
claims.note: Traffic offences are prosecuted directly in court; administrative procedure acts do not require prior agency hearings for citations.

claims.text: City traffic ordinances bind only city residents
claims.note: Municipal traffic ordinances apply to anyone driving within city limits, resident or not.

claims.text: Sovereign citizens send threats to judges and court officials
claims.note: The FBI is quoted saying members threaten judges, law enforcement and government personnel.

claims.text: A sincere belief in the right to travel defeats traffic charges for lack of criminal intent
claims.note: Driving without a license is typically a strict-liability or general-intent offence, and mistake of law is no defence.

claims.text: A driver's license is a contract that is void without full disclosure and knowing consent
claims.note: A license is a regulatory permit, not a contract, and courts reject contract-based challenges to it.

claims.text: Private UCC filings have seized and dissolved the US government corporation
claims.note: OPPT promoters claimed UCC filings had 'foreclosed' governments and banks and promised $10 billion in gold each; nothing was delivered and they blamed aliens.

claims.text: Original land titles were deliberately destroyed in the 1814 burning of Washington to erase sovereign ownership
claims.note: Deeds are kept by county recorders, and the 1814 fire destroyed federal buildings and the Library of Congress, not the nation's land titles.

claims.text: The 1871 District of Columbia territorial government was abolished within a few years
claims.note: The 1871 District government 'lasted until June 20, 1874', when an act abolished it and put the District under appointed commissioners.

claims.text: Incorporating a city government makes it a municipal corporation, not a for-profit business
claims.note: The Court explains that a municipal corporation is a subordinate agency of the state or government that created it, exercising delegated public powers; it is not a private business.

claims.text: Refusing a ticket for fraud or denying your signature on it gets traffic charges dismissed
claims.note: Courts do not dismiss citations because a defendant rejects or disowns them; reported dismissals have ordinary causes.

claims.text: Sending certified-mail notices to officials makes code enforcement stop
claims.note: Notices and affidavits have no legal effect on permit or code enforcement; a lull in letters is an anecdote.

claims.text: You can get a US passport without giving a Social Security number
claims.note: The State Department can issue a passport without an SSN, but the IRS may fine the applicant and it confers no special status.

claims.text: QAnon followers adopted sovereign-citizen claims such as a March 4 inauguration
claims.note: News reports in early 2021 documented QAnon channels promoting the 1871-based March 4 inauguration claim.

claims.text: Sovereign-citizen ideology is rooted in white nationalism and antisemitism
claims.note: Its Posse Comitatus origins were racist and antisemitic, but today's movement includes many adherents, such as Moorish groups, without those beliefs.

claims.text: Prosecutors sometimes drop minor charges against disruptive defendants to save court time
claims.note: Prosecutorial discretion commonly drops low-value cases, though how often disruption drives it is not measured.

claims.text: A published declaration of non-consent binds officials and makes them liable for interfering with you
claims.note: Unilateral declarations that withdraw consent from government and courts (NOUICR), deemed accepted unless rebutted, were implicitly rejected as legally baseless.

claims.text: Statutory definitions of "person" cover only corporations or people acting in a commercial capacity
claims.note: IRC 7701(a)(1) defines 'person' to include an individual as well as trusts, estates, partnerships and corporations; arguments that an individual is not a 'person' are uniformly rejected.

claims.text: Vehicle registration and certificate of title requirements apply only to vehicles used commercially
claims.note: A private citizen driving his own car was validly convicted for lacking registration; states may require registration of 'all motor vehicles - those moving in interstate commerce as well as others'.

claims.text: State reception statutes make the common law supreme over conflicting statutes
claims.note: Reception statutes adopt English common law only where not inconsistent with state statutes, so statutes prevail.

claims.text: The federal definition of motor vehicle as a commercial contrivance governs state driver licensing laws
claims.note: Absent national legislation a state may set its own rules for all motor vehicles on its highways; state licensing rests on state police power, not on a federal commercial definition.

claims.text: Removing or bypassing a utility meter lets you stop paying for energy
claims.note: Meter tampering is abstracting electricity, a crime, and the supply charges remain owed.

claims.text: Admiralty or maritime law applies to ordinary people outside shipping matters
claims.note: Admiralty jurisdiction covers ships, cargo and navigable waters, not traffic, tax or criminal cases against individuals.

claims.text: Self-represented litigants are held to the same procedural rules as lawyers
claims.note: The court warned the pro se defendant, with appellate approval, that he would be held to the same rules of evidence and procedure as if represented by an attorney.

claims.text: Sovereign citizens reject the legitimacy of federal and state authority over them
claims.note: The court describes the hallmark of the movement as believing oneself sovereign, not a US citizen and not subject to government authority, used to avoid taxes, debts and prosecution.

claims.text: Living by sovereign-citizen beliefs costs adherents jobs, homes, family ties and jail time
claims.note: The authors say pseudolaw causes self-inflicted harm: higher damages and costs, criminal sanctions, psychiatric detention, foreclosed homes and broken families.

claims.text: A state-citizen passport ends tickets, taxes, debt collection and foreclosure for the holder
claims.note: A passport has no effect on tax, traffic or debt obligations; people relying on this are prosecuted and foreclosed on.

claims.text: Ignoring a lawsuit cannot lead to a default judgment against a state citizen
claims.note: Failing to answer a properly served suit leads to default judgment for anyone, whatever status they claim.

claims.text: A state citizen and a US citizen are different statuses, and US citizens have no constitutional rights
claims.note: The 14th Amendment makes people born in the US citizens of both the US and their state at once; the Tax Court called state-but-not-US citizenship 'nonsensical' and US citizenship paramount.

claims.text: Answering "no" to US citizenship on a passport application makes you a state citizen instead
claims.note: Citizenship or nationality is fixed by place and parentage of birth, and a valid US passport is conclusive proof of US citizenship; nothing lets a form answer create a separate 'state citizen' status.

claims.text: A crime requires an injured party, so victimless offences cannot be prosecuted
claims.note: Convictions for failure to display license and plate, offenses with no injured party, were affirmed over the argument that these are not common-law crimes.

claims.text: The US federal government has declared bankruptcy
claims.note: The federal government has never filed for or been placed in bankruptcy; it has kept borrowing, taxing and paying debts.

claims.text: Sending a creditor a tender of payment or negotiable instrument that it refuses discharges the debt
claims.note: The court rejected the argument that a bill of exchange not returned within 72 hours counts as honored; the case cited says nothing of the kind and the debt was not discharged.

claims.text: A creditor's silence in response to your notices means it has accepted your terms
claims.note: No UCC provision makes failure to answer an 'Affidavit of Truth' within ten days an admission; a party cannot create a duty to respond by declaring one in a notarized document.

claims.text: Drivers can lawfully refuse to hand police their license, registration and insurance at a traffic stop
claims.note: Ohio R.C. 4507.35 requires an operator to display the license or proof on a peace officer's demand; refusal led to an affirmed conviction.

claims.text: Every traffic stop is a custodial arrest that requires Miranda warnings
claims.note: Berkemer v. McCarty held that routine traffic stops are not custodial for Miranda purposes.

claims.text: Stopping mortgage and loan payments on sovereign-citizen grounds leads to foreclosure and repossession
claims.note: Lenders foreclose and repossess on default regardless of pseudolegal notices, which courts disregard.

claims.text: Right-to-travel materials quote court rulings out of context
claims.note: The stock citations (Thompson v. Smith, Chicago Motor Coach) concern other issues and themselves allow road regulation.

claims.text: Signing with a symbol inside a box means no binding contract is formed
claims.note: Any mark made with intent to sign binds the signer; the four-corners rule concerns evidence, not signatures.

claims.text: Banks keep the checks you write and sell them as securities on the market
claims.note: Checks stopped coming back because of image clearing under Check 21; they are not bundled into securities.

claims.text: A secret continuity-of-government plan is dissolving the US corporation to restore the original republic
claims.note: No such plan exists; the 'United States Corporation Company' cited is a private registered-agent firm, not the government.

claims.text: Homeowners in arrears can often avoid repossession by showing a realistic plan to clear the arrears
claims.note: Under UK law courts can adjourn or suspend possession where arrears can be cleared in a reasonable period, and often do.

claims.text: Outside of driving, many states do not require a person stopped by police to identify themselves
claims.note: Roughly half the states have stop-and-identify laws upheld in Hiibel; the rest impose no general duty on pedestrians.

claims.text: Giving police a false identity is a crime even where you may stay silent
claims.note: Every state criminalizes false identification to officers, separately from any duty to identify.

claims.text: Most sovereign citizens are nonviolent and act mainly through vexatious litigation and paperwork
claims.note: Only a small fraction of OPCA believers have turned to violence; their main tool is a 'competition of laws' fought through the courts.

commonlyWrong.text: The government creates a separate corporate entity, the strawman, in your all-caps name
commonlyWrong.note: The strawman concept 'has no basis in law in either the US or Canada -- it is simply a myth', and courts have said so time and again.

commonlyWrong.text: Declaring yourself an American State National removes you from federal and state statutory jurisdiction
commonlyWrong.note: Circuits rejected claims that being a citizen of a state or 'state republic' rather than the US puts one beyond federal court jurisdiction (2d Cir. Drachenberg, 7th Cir. Hilgeford); federal tax context only, so state jurisdiction is not covered.

commonlyWrong.text: A constitutional right to travel means a private person needs no driver's license to drive a private car
commonlyWrong.note: The Supreme Court upheld conviction of a man driving his own car from his office into Maryland without the required registration; licensing private drivers is valid police power.

commonlyWrong.text: Signing with "UCC 1-308" or "without prejudice" stops a court from binding you to the law
commonlyWrong.note: UCC 1-308's text and official comment: it lets a party keep performing a commercial contract under protest during a dispute without waiving reserved rights. It says nothing about courts or criminal law.

commonlyWrong.text: Using a car for private travel rather than commerce is not driving under the motor vehicle laws
commonlyWrong.note: A driver with a homemade 'private' plate who claimed a right to travel privately without a license was convicted of license and plate offenses, affirmed on appeal.

commonlyWrong.text: Statutes are contracts or corporate policy that bind only people who consent to them
commonlyWrong.note: A freeman who said he never consented to NZ's Land Transport Act had his appeal struck out as an abuse of process; Shaw v AG (WA) held a Constitution Act is a statute, not a contract.

commonlyWrong.text: Courts have ruled that a license is not required to travel by automobile
commonlyWrong.note: The court cites its own and other courts' repeated rejection of right-to-travel-without-a-license arguments. The rulings run the other way.

commonlyWrong.text: The United States became a private corporation under the District of Columbia Act of 1871
commonlyWrong.note: The Supreme Court describes the 1871 Act as making the District of Columbia 'a body corporate for municipal purposes', a mere municipal corporation; sovereign power over the District stays with the US government and Congress.

commonlyWrong.text: A birth certificate is a bond or security traded to fund a secret account in your name
commonlyWrong.note: Treasury says a birth certificate has no monetary value, cannot be used for purchases or to claim bonds, and the 'Exemption Account' is fictitious and does not exist in the Treasury system.

commonlyWrong.text: Courts have no jurisdiction over you unless you consent or contract with them
commonlyWrong.note: The Seventh Circuit holds that whatever status a person claims (sovereign citizen, secured-party creditor, flesh-and-blood human), that person is not beyond the courts' jurisdiction; the defendants' insistence that they did not consent changed nothing and they were tried and convicted.

commonlyWrong.text: The government pledged its citizens and their property as collateral for its debts to bankers
commonlyWrong.note: The court sets out the theory that citizens are pledged as security for the national debt and rejects it as revisionist history and conspiracy theory; the authorities cited only concern leaving the gold standard.

commonlyWrong.text: Since the 1933 gold suspension, money is credit and debts cannot be lawfully paid, only discharged
commonlyWrong.note: HJR 192 declares US currency legal tender for all debts and measures obligations in dollars; the court says it addresses only the move off gold and supports no theory of discharge rather than payment.

commonlyWrong.text: State national paperwork or passports protect the holder from being detained by police
commonlyWrong.note: US passports confer no immunity; state-national documents carry no legal weight and holders are arrested like anyone else.

commonlyWrong.text: A land patent gives an owner allodial title that protects the property from taxes and foreclosure
commonlyWrong.note: The Seventh Circuit called a self-drafted 'land patent' recorded to defeat a mortgage a blatant attempt to improve title by personal fiat; it did not improve title, foreclosure stood, and the court imposed sanctions for a frivolous appeal.

commonlyWrong.text: You can draw on a secret Treasury account to pay debts by writing "accepted for value" on bills
commonlyWrong.note: Citing the 6th Circuit (Anderson), the Treasury does not maintain depository accounts against which an individual can draw; secret per-citizen accounts are 'pure fantasy' and fictitious instruments can be prosecuted under 18 USC 514.

commonlyWrong.text: Common law, the Magna Carta or natural law override statutes for a free person who rejects them
commonlyWrong.note: All but three provisions of Magna Carta were repealed by 1969, and the High Court of Australia held in 1905 that invalidity for nonconformity with Magna Carta is 'not one for serious refutation'; McHugh J called it political ideals that do not bind parliaments.

commonlyWrong.text: The US federal government is a private corporation rather than a lawful sovereign government
commonlyWrong.note: A district court held the United States is a sovereign, not a corporation, and called contrary arguments wholly frivolous; the Tax Court sanctioned a taxpayer arguing 'the United States is a corporation'; trial-level rulings.

commonlyWrong.text: Filing a UCC-1 financing statement gives you ownership and control of your strawman
commonlyWrong.note: Filing UCC-1 statements with birth certificates to 'redeem' the straw man is a frivolous redemption theory that courts call implausible and clearly nonsense.

commonlyWrong.text: Ordinary wages are not taxable income under federal law
commonlyWrong.note: IRC 61 defines gross income to include compensation for services, and appellate courts (e.g. 3d Cir. Connor: every court has unequivocally rejected the argument that wages are not income) sanction the contrary argument.

commonlyWrong.text: A person can ignore a licensing law that restricts a constitutional right and act with impunity
commonlyWrong.note: Licensing does not unlawfully restrict the right to travel; the defendant who ignored it was convicted and the convictions were affirmed.

commonlyWrong.text: Recording expatriation and name declarations at a land records office legally changes your political status
commonlyWrong.note: Recorders accept documents without validating them; citizenship status changes only through federal renunciation procedures.

commonlyWrong.text: Refusing to show a license or identify yourself at a traffic stop gets you released rather than arrested
commonlyWrong.note: A driver who refused license, registration and name was removed from the car, arrested and convicted of obstruction, failure to disclose and failure to display; one case.

commonlyWrong.text: A traffic ticket is an offer to contract that you can refuse
commonlyWrong.note: In Ohio the uniform traffic ticket serves as the complaint and summons, a charging document rather than an offer to contract.

commonlyWrong.text: A warranty deed is only colour of title and gives no real ownership
commonlyWrong.note: A warranty deed conveys full legal title from the grantor; the original patent passes with the chain of title automatically.

commonlyWrong.text: The 14th Amendment made Americans corporate persons or property of the federal government
commonlyWrong.note: The amendment conferred citizenship and equal protection; it created no corporate status or second-class citizen.

commonlyWrong.text: Answering "no" to US citizenship on a passport application makes you a state citizen instead
commonlyWrong.note: Citizenship or nationality is fixed by place and parentage of birth, and a valid US passport is conclusive proof of US citizenship; nothing lets a form answer create a separate 'state citizen' status.

commonlyWrong.text: Any contract can be cancelled during a legally guaranteed three- or seven-day cooling-off period
commonlyWrong.note: Cooling-off rights exist only for specific transactions such as door-to-door sales or some loans, not contracts in general.

commonlyWrong.text: Challenging a court's jurisdiction and demanding proof of a contract gets traffic tickets dismissed
commonlyWrong.note: The defendant's notice to abate, sovereignty affidavit and jurisdiction challenge were summarily overruled and he was convicted on all traffic and related charges; one case.

commonlyWrong.text: A crime requires an injured party, so victimless offences cannot be prosecuted
commonlyWrong.note: Convictions for failure to display license and plate, offenses with no injured party, were affirmed over the argument that these are not common-law crimes.

commonlyWrong.text: A driver's license is a contract that is void without full disclosure and knowing consent
commonlyWrong.note: A license is a regulatory permit, not a contract, and courts reject contract-based challenges to it.

commonlyWrong.text: The US federal government has declared bankruptcy
commonlyWrong.note: The federal government has never filed for or been placed in bankruptcy; it has kept borrowing, taxing and paying debts.

commonlyWrong.text: Filing a Form 1099-OID lets you claim money back from the Treasury
commonlyWrong.note: Form 1099-OID only reports interest income; it is not a financial instrument or a way to withdraw money from the Treasury, and the 8th Circuit upheld convictions for 1099-OID refund schemes.

commonlyWrong.text: The Fourteenth Amendment was never lawfully ratified
commonlyWrong.note: The 14th Amendment was certified in 1868 and courts have rejected challenges to its ratification.

commonlyWrong.text: An officer who makes a traffic stop with emergency lights for a non-emergency commits a felony
commonlyWrong.note: Police may use lights to make lawful traffic stops; no statute makes that a felony.

commonlyWrong.text: Paying income tax is voluntary
commonlyWrong.note: IRC 1 imposes the tax and 6151 requires payment; 'voluntary' in Flora refers to self-assessment, and multiple circuits (8th Drefke, 9th Wilcox, 2d Banat) reject the voluntary-payment argument as frivolous with sanctions.

commonlyWrong.text: Renouncing US citizenship or claiming state national status exempts you from federal income tax
commonlyWrong.note: Claims to be solely a citizen of a sovereign state and not subject to federal tax are uniformly rejected (14th Amendment gives simultaneous state and federal citizenship); the document does not address formal expatriation, so this judges the state-national prong.

commonlyWrong.text: A state citizen and a US citizen are different statuses, and US citizens have no constitutional rights
commonlyWrong.note: The 14th Amendment makes people born in the US citizens of both the US and their state at once; the Tax Court called state-but-not-US citizenship 'nonsensical' and US citizenship paramount.

commonlyWrong.text: Suing police over a right-to-travel arrest wins large damage awards
commonlyWrong.note: Section 1983 suits on right-to-travel theories are dismissed as frivolous, for example Ford v. Anones.

commonlyWrong.text: Your signature creates the credit a lender extends, making you the true creditor
commonlyWrong.note: The claim that the borrower creates the loaned money by signature is called erroneous; the one supporting case (Credit River, 1968) was declared a nullity and rejected in Commonwealth courts.

commonlyWrong.text: All driver's licenses are commercial licenses
commonlyWrong.note: States issue distinct non-commercial and commercial (CDL) licenses; an ordinary license confers no commercial status.

commonlyWrong.text: Americans are misidentified at birth as federal citizens through deceptive hospital paperwork
commonlyWrong.note: Under the Fourteenth Amendment persons born in the US and subject to its jurisdiction are citizens at birth by operation of law, not by hospital paperwork.

commonlyWrong.text: Arguing the right to travel in traffic court gets no-plates tickets dismissed
commonlyWrong.note: The right-to-travel defendant was convicted of failure to display a license plate, and the appeal court affirmed; one case.

commonlyWrong.text: Banks keep the checks you write and sell them as securities on the market
commonlyWrong.note: Checks stopped coming back because of image clearing under Check 21; they are not bundled into securities.

commonlyWrong.text: Becoming a citizen forfeits all your property and labour to the state
commonlyWrong.note: Citizenship statutes confer status; they transfer no property, and citizens own property in their own names under ordinary law.

commonlyWrong.text: A borrower owes a bank nothing unless the bank can prove it suffered a loss on the loan
commonlyWrong.note: A loan contract obliges repayment whether or not the lender sold the note; vapour-money arguments are uniformly rejected.

commonlyWrong.text: Bracketing contract terms you disagree with removes them from the contract
commonlyWrong.note: Unilateral marks do not alter a contract unless the other party agrees; style manuals have no legal effect.

commonlyWrong.text: Citizen-convened common-law grand juries have legal authority to check government
commonlyWrong.note: Only grand juries summoned by courts under statute have legal power; self-convened ones have none.

commonlyWrong.text: Citizens are creditors of the government and can use the debt it owes them to discharge their own debts
commonlyWrong.note: The claim that a person can use the government's supposed debt to her to discharge debts to third parties by a bill of exchange was rejected; the tender was worthless and the foreclosure was lawful.

commonlyWrong.text: US citizens under the Fourteenth Amendment have no access to the Bill of Rights
commonlyWrong.note: Courts apply the Bill of Rights to all citizens, and the 14th Amendment incorporated most of it against the states.

commonlyWrong.text: City traffic ordinances bind only city residents
commonlyWrong.note: Municipal traffic ordinances apply to anyone driving within city limits, resident or not.

commonlyWrong.text: Closed bank accounts can be used to pay debts by electronic transfer or setoff
commonlyWrong.note: Payments drawn on closed accounts bounce and are reversed; knowingly using them is fraud.

commonlyWrong.text: A company's refusal to accept a UCC 1-308 signature proves the reservation has legal force
commonlyWrong.note: A company declining altered contract terms shows only caution about its arbitration clause, not that the notation exempts anyone from law.

commonlyWrong.text: Congress pledged the United States to foreign bankers in 1871 to cover Civil War debts
commonlyWrong.note: No 1871 statute or record shows such a pledge; Civil War debt was financed by public bonds.

commonlyWrong.text: Constitutional amendments ratified after 1871, including the income tax amendment, are void
commonlyWrong.note: The 16th Amendment was ratified by 40+ states and certified in 1913; courts hold the certification conclusive and reject non-ratification claims, so the income tax amendment is valid (only that amendment is covered).

commonlyWrong.text: A contract is not legally binding unless both parties understand and agree to every term
commonlyWrong.note: Courts enforce signed standard-form contracts whether or not the signer read or understood every term.

commonlyWrong.text: A county recorder who refuses sovereign filings can be claimed against personally through their surety bond
commonlyWrong.note: Official bonds cover real misconduct; refusing bogus filings is lawful and such bond claims fail.

commonlyWrong.text: A creditor's silence in response to your notices means it has accepted your terms
commonlyWrong.note: No UCC provision makes failure to answer an 'Affidavit of Truth' within ten days an admission; a party cannot create a duty to respond by declaring one in a notarized document.

commonlyWrong.text: Declaring yourself a living man rather than a legal person places you outside the jurisdiction of the law
commonlyWrong.note: Appellate court: a 'flesh-and-blood human being' or 'sovereign citizen' is not beyond the courts' jurisdiction, and such theories 'should be rejected summarily, however they are presented'.

commonlyWrong.text: Driver licensing and registration exist mainly to extract money for the DMV and insurers
commonlyWrong.note: The Court found the purpose was public safety and order plus compensation for costly roads, and held the statute 'is not a mere revenue measure'.

commonlyWrong.text: Drivers can lawfully refuse to hand police their license, registration and insurance at a traffic stop
commonlyWrong.note: Ohio R.C. 4507.35 requires an operator to display the license or proof on a peace officer's demand; refusal led to an affirmed conviction.

commonlyWrong.text: Equity and trust filings can recover your property from a public trust the state holds it in
commonlyWrong.note: No public trust holds citizens' property; pseudolegal trust filings have no effect and courts dismiss them.

commonlyWrong.text: Every traffic stop is a custodial arrest that requires Miranda warnings
commonlyWrong.note: Berkemer v. McCarty held that routine traffic stops are not custodial for Miranda purposes.

commonlyWrong.text: The federal definition of motor vehicle as a commercial contrivance governs state driver licensing laws
commonlyWrong.note: Absent national legislation a state may set its own rules for all motor vehicles on its highways; state licensing rests on state police power, not on a federal commercial definition.

commonlyWrong.text: Federal income tax paid to the IRS goes to a foreign corporation rather than the US Treasury
commonlyWrong.note: The IRS is organised under the Secretary of the Treasury to administer the internal revenue laws, not a private or foreign corporation; the document does not trace where receipts are deposited.

commonlyWrong.text: Federal motor-carrier rules that exempt private drivers show state traffic laws reach only commercial drivers
commonlyWrong.note: FMCSA rules govern interstate carriers only; state traffic codes separately cover all drivers, and courts reject reading one through the other.

commonlyWrong.text: The Federal Reserve is a private corporation that owns the currency it issues
commonlyWrong.note: Regional reserve banks have member-bank stockholders, but the Fed is a government-created system and its notes are obligations of the United States.

commonlyWrong.text: Filing a UCC-1 financing statement on your strawman name releases you from its debts and obligations
commonlyWrong.note: The plaintiff filed UCC-1/UCC-3 statements naming herself as secured party over her all-caps 'fictitious entity', yet her mortgage debt was not discharged and her claims were dismissed with prejudice.
