commonlyWrong.text: Giving police your name or information creates a contract with them
commonlyWrong.note: Identifying yourself to police forms no contract; police authority comes from statute, not agreement.

commonlyWrong.text: Giving up a social insurance or social security number frees a person from income tax
commonlyWrong.note: Tax liability depends on income and residence, not on holding an identifying number.

commonlyWrong.text: A gold-fringed flag means a courtroom is operating under admiralty or maritime law
commonlyWrong.note: The court reviews flag law: fringe is not part of the flag, has no heraldic or legal significance, and cannot change a court's jurisdiction, which 'is a matter of law, statute, and constitution'. It cites several courts calling the argument frivolous.

commonlyWrong.text: The government creates large sums of money against each person's Social Security number
commonlyWrong.note: Treasury: there is no monetary value to a birth certificate or social security number, and TreasuryDirect accounts only hold what the owner funds from their own bank account.

commonlyWrong.text: Handing your driver's license to an officer consents to being treated as a commercial driver
commonlyWrong.note: Ordinary licenses are non-commercial and showing one creates no commercial status or contract.

commonlyWrong.text: Hiring a lawyer automatically gives the court jurisdiction over you
commonlyWrong.note: The court cites precedent that federal courts have subject-matter and personal jurisdiction over defendants brought before them on federal indictments; jurisdiction comes from the indictment and law, not from hiring counsel.

commonlyWrong.text: Ignoring a lawsuit cannot lead to a default judgment against a state citizen
commonlyWrong.note: Failing to answer a properly served suit leads to default judgment for anyone, whatever status they claim.

commonlyWrong.text: Income tax is a franchise fee owed only by people who accept state-created legal personhood
commonlyWrong.note: The 10th Circuit upheld penalties for arguing that the income tax is an excise on privileged activities, and IRC 1 taxes individuals' income regardless of claimed status.

commonlyWrong.text: Income tax was illegal under the original Constitution
commonlyWrong.note: The original Constitution allowed income taxes if apportioned and the Civil War income tax was upheld; the 16th Amendment removed apportionment.

commonlyWrong.text: The ink colour used to sign a document changes its legal effect
commonlyWrong.note: No law gives signature ink colour any legal meaning.

commonlyWrong.text: The IRS is a private corporation chartered in Delaware, not part of the Treasury
commonlyWrong.note: The IRS is an agency created under the Treasury Secretary's IRC 7801 authority with a Commissioner under 7803; the 11th Circuit held it is clearly an agency of the United States and courts call the private-corporation claim wholly frivolous.

commonlyWrong.text: Juries can throw out any law they find unjust through jury nullification
commonlyWrong.note: Criminal juries can acquit against the evidence, but that sets no precedent and does not void any law, and judges may remove jurors who announce it.

commonlyWrong.text: Legislators have no authority to regulate the behaviour of the people
commonlyWrong.note: The Constitution grants legislative power and states have broad police power to regulate conduct.

commonlyWrong.text: A lender's failure to explain how your signature creates credit is fraud that voids the debt
commonlyWrong.note: Truth in Lending requires disclosure of credit terms, not this theory; courts dismiss nondisclosure-of-credit-creation claims.

commonlyWrong.text: A lost Titles of Nobility 13th Amendment strips lawyers and judges of citizenship and voids the courts
commonlyWrong.note: The Titles of Nobility Amendment was never ratified, and courts reject the argument.

commonlyWrong.text: Magna Carta Article 61 gives people a lawful right to refuse laws they deem invalid
commonlyWrong.note: Clause 61 was annulled within months in 1215 and never reissued; UK courts reject 'lawful rebellion' defences.

commonlyWrong.text: Millions of Americans have formally changed their status to American State National
commonlyWrong.note: There is no legal status change to record; the figure is unsourced and no government recognises such corrections.

commonlyWrong.text: A mortgage is void because the bank created the loan money from nothing
commonlyWrong.note: 'Banks loan nothing of value because they create money from thin air' is erroneous; Credit River, which denied a bank recovery on that basis, was declared a nullity and rejected in Australian and Canadian courts.

commonlyWrong.text: Officers who detain a state national face large personal fines payable to the detainee
commonlyWrong.note: No law sets such fines; self-styled fee schedules are unenforceable and suits on them are dismissed.

commonlyWrong.text: The original US Constitution was replaced in 1871 by a separate corporate constitution
commonlyWrong.note: The 1871 Act only set up a municipal government for the District, with powers 'not inconsistent with the constitution and laws of the United States'. It replaced no constitution and was itself abolished in 1874.

commonlyWrong.text: Original land titles were deliberately destroyed in the 1814 burning of Washington to erase sovereign ownership
commonlyWrong.note: Deeds are kept by county recorders, and the 1814 fire destroyed federal buildings and the Library of Congress, not the nation's land titles.

commonlyWrong.text: Owning land in fee simple or allodium exempts it from property tax
commonlyWrong.note: Fee simple land is taxed everywhere in the US and courts and attorneys general reject allodial-title tax exemptions.

commonlyWrong.text: Persistent pseudolegal administrative filings get creditors to drop claims or offer favorable settlements
commonlyWrong.note: Only sellers' anecdotes support it; creditors usually proceed and courts disregard such records.

commonlyWrong.text: The president has ruled under continuous unconstitutional emergency powers since 1933
commonlyWrong.note: The 1976 National Emergencies Act ended the old emergencies; current emergencies are specific, statutory and reviewable.

commonlyWrong.text: Private UCC filings have seized and dissolved the US government corporation
commonlyWrong.note: OPPT promoters claimed UCC filings had 'foreclosed' governments and banks and promised $10 billion in gold each; nothing was delivered and they blamed aliens.

commonlyWrong.text: A properly secured land patent has never lost in an appellate court
commonlyWrong.note: Appellate courts repeatedly reject land-patent defences to taxes and foreclosure, e.g. Hilgeford v. Peoples Bank.

commonlyWrong.text: Pseudolegal loopholes let homeowners walk away from mortgage obligations
commonlyWrong.note: Because the bill of exchange was not valid payment, the lender 'was within [its] rights to foreclose'; all claims were dismissed with prejudice.

commonlyWrong.text: A published declaration of non-consent binds officials and makes them liable for interfering with you
commonlyWrong.note: Unilateral declarations that withdraw consent from government and courts (NOUICR), deemed accepted unless rebutted, were implicitly rejected as legally baseless.

commonlyWrong.text: Reclaiming state national status restores your rights and control over your property
commonlyWrong.note: The paperwork has no legal effect on rights or property; courts ignore it.

commonlyWrong.text: Reconstruction never ended and the US remains under a foreign military government
commonlyWrong.note: Reconstruction ended in 1877 and civilian constitutional government has operated since; the claim has no documentary basis.

commonlyWrong.text: Redemption paperwork lets people erase all their personal debts
commonlyWrong.note: Redemption instruments (1099-OID, bonded notes, sight drafts on a Treasury account) are no legitimate method of paying any public or private debt, and using them risks criminal charges.

commonlyWrong.text: Refusing a ticket for fraud or denying your signature on it gets traffic charges dismissed
commonlyWrong.note: Courts do not dismiss citations because a defendant rejects or disowns them; reported dismissals have ordinary causes.

commonlyWrong.text: Registering a car, property or child signs ownership over to the government
commonlyWrong.note: Registration records ownership or a birth; it does not transfer title to the state.

commonlyWrong.text: A secret continuity-of-government plan is dissolving the US corporation to restore the original republic
commonlyWrong.note: No such plan exists; the 'United States Corporation Company' cited is a private registered-agent firm, not the government.

commonlyWrong.text: Self-convened common-law courts have real legal authority to try and sentence officials
commonlyWrong.note: Such bodies have no legal standing; their verdicts are unenforceable and acting on them can itself be a crime.

commonlyWrong.text: Sending certified-mail notices to officials makes code enforcement stop
commonlyWrong.note: Notices and affidavits have no legal effect on permit or code enforcement; a lull in letters is an anecdote.

commonlyWrong.text: Sending a creditor a tender of payment or negotiable instrument that it refuses discharges the debt
commonlyWrong.note: The court rejected the argument that a bill of exchange not returned within 72 hours counts as honored; the case cited says nothing of the kind and the debt was not discharged.

commonlyWrong.text: Serving a notice of claim of right on the government gives lawful excuse to disobey statutes
commonlyWrong.note: The Freeman 'Notice of Understanding, Intent, and Claim of Right' is meant to withdraw consent, but unilateral rejection of state authority was refused leave as having no legal merit.

commonlyWrong.text: Signing a contract "all rights reserved UCC 1-308" keeps you from being bound as the debtor
commonlyWrong.note: 1-308 only keeps rights a party reserves while it performs or assents to performance; it is about continuing performance despite a dispute, not escaping the obligation as debtor.

commonlyWrong.text: Signing a mortgage or opening a bank account signs away your rights through a power of attorney
commonlyWrong.note: Mortgages and account agreements are ordinary contracts with defined terms; they grant no general power of attorney.

commonlyWrong.text: Signing with a symbol inside a box means no binding contract is formed
commonlyWrong.note: Any mark made with intent to sign binds the signer; the four-corners rule concerns evidence, not signatures.

commonlyWrong.text: A sincere belief in the right to travel defeats traffic charges for lack of criminal intent
commonlyWrong.note: Driving without a license is typically a strict-liability or general-intent offence, and mistake of law is no defence.

commonlyWrong.text: Speeding laws apply only to commercial drivers, not private travellers
commonlyWrong.note: Speed limits apply to every driver on public roads; courts reject the commercial-only reading.

commonlyWrong.text: A state cannot charge a licence fee for exercising a constitutional right, so licensing private travel is unconstitutional
commonlyWrong.note: The Supreme Court upheld registration and operator license fees graduated by horsepower as a valid police-power measure and fair compensation for roads, not a violation of the right to pass through the state.

commonlyWrong.text: A state-citizen passport ends tickets, taxes, debt collection and foreclosure for the holder
commonlyWrong.note: A passport has no effect on tax, traffic or debt obligations; people relying on this are prosecuted and foreclosed on.

commonlyWrong.text: State jural assemblies of state nationals hold lawful judicial authority
commonlyWrong.note: These assemblies have no legal standing; their 'courts' and rulings are unrecognised and members have been prosecuted for acting on them.

commonlyWrong.text: State reception statutes make the common law supreme over conflicting statutes
commonlyWrong.note: Reception statutes adopt English common law only where not inconsistent with state statutes, so statutes prevail.

commonlyWrong.text: Statutory definitions of "person" cover only corporations or people acting in a commercial capacity
commonlyWrong.note: IRC 7701(a)(1) defines 'person' to include an individual as well as trusts, estates, partnerships and corporations; arguments that an individual is not a 'person' are uniformly rejected.

commonlyWrong.text: Surrendering your driver's license and having no ID on file leaves police unable to prosecute you
commonlyWrong.note: Police can detain and book unidentified people and prosecute under fingerprints or a John Doe name; refusing ID usually adds charges.

commonlyWrong.text: Tax authorities back off people who refuse to pay on sovereign grounds rather than risk a public court loss
commonlyWrong.note: Most charged protesters are convicted, and even after an acquittal the IRS may still pursue the underlying tax and civil penalties; the document lists many pursued cases.

commonlyWrong.text: The tax code's definition of person means the law treats you as a corporation
commonlyWrong.note: The tax code's 'person' expressly includes an individual alongside corporations, so being a 'person' does not make one a corporation; courts reject the not-a-person argument.

commonlyWrong.text: Taxation of individuals is illegal
commonlyWrong.note: The 16th Amendment authorizes a non-apportioned income tax on US citizens; the Supreme Court upheld it in Brushaber and courts have consistently rejected challenges.

commonlyWrong.text: Telling a court you are not the legal person named in the charges makes prosecutors drop them
commonlyWrong.note: Defendants who said they were a living man and not the named person all lost; the court found them identifiable by the legal name.

commonlyWrong.text: Traffic cases against private travellers are dismissed for lack of jurisdiction when commerce is not proven
commonlyWrong.note: The state argued the driver was not in commerce at all, and his conviction was affirmed; state motor vehicle rules reach all vehicles on its highways, so no commerce needs to be proved.

commonlyWrong.text: Traffic cases are civil administrative matters that fail unless the state first holds an agency hearing
commonlyWrong.note: Traffic offences are prosecuted directly in court; administrative procedure acts do not require prior agency hearings for citations.

commonlyWrong.text: The United States remains a colony of the British Crown or the Vatican
commonlyWrong.note: Britain recognised US independence in the 1783 Treaty of Paris; no legal authority supports continuing Crown or Vatican control.

commonlyWrong.text: An unrebutted notarized affidavit is the highest truth in law and binds the agency that receives it
commonlyWrong.note: The court found no authority that maxims like 'an unrebutted affidavit stands as truth in commerce' have binding force, and held that non-response created no estoppel.

commonlyWrong.text: Vehicle registration and certificate of title requirements apply only to vehicles used commercially
commonlyWrong.note: A private citizen driving his own car was validly convicted for lacking registration; states may require registration of 'all motor vehicles - those moving in interstate commerce as well as others'.

commonlyWrong.text: Without re-securing the land patent, a prior claimant can evict you from land you bought
commonlyWrong.note: Title passes through recorded deeds; a patent cannot be reclaimed by a prior owner to evict a later buyer.

commonlyWrong.text: Writing a name in all capitals in a legal document marks it as a corporation
commonlyWrong.note: The Tax Court (Holmes) dismissed as frivolous the claim that IRS letters addressed in all capitals treat the taxpayer as a fictional corporate entity, and imposed a $10,000 penalty.

commonlyWrong.text: Writing "UCC 1-308 refused" on a ticket and returning it within three days voids it
commonlyWrong.note: The section covers performance under reservation of rights in commercial dealings; it contains no time limit and no mechanism for voiding citations.

commonlyWrong.text: Writing your name in lowercase or with special punctuation changes your legal status
commonlyWrong.note: Litigants styled as 'scott-william of the house of Larsen' or 'S-I-R-Crown' were unsuccessful; the legal name still identified them.

commonlyWrong.text: Admiralty or maritime law applies to ordinary people outside shipping matters
commonlyWrong.note: Admiralty jurisdiction covers ships, cargo and navigable waters, not traffic, tax or criminal cases against individuals.

commonlyWrong.text: Birth certificates carry CUSIP numbers that show they are registered securities
commonlyWrong.note: CUSIPs identify registered securities; numbers on birth certificates are state file numbers, and no birth-certificate securities exist.

commonlyWrong.text: The Constitution was never validly ratified and the Articles of Confederation still govern
commonlyWrong.note: The Constitution was ratified in 1788 and replaced the Articles; every court applies it.

commonlyWrong.text: Court orders without a wet-ink signature or court seal are void
commonlyWrong.note: Courts issue valid orders electronically and without seals; judges uniformly reject the wet-ink argument.

commonlyWrong.text: Federal law applies only in the District of Columbia, federal territories and enclaves
commonlyWrong.note: Courts uniformly reject the argument that the US consists only of DC, territories and enclaves; 7th, 6th, 9th and 11th Circuits called it frivolous and the 16th Amendment tax applies nationwide.

commonlyWrong.text: Gold fringe on a US flag signals that martial law is in effect
commonlyWrong.note: No law requires or forbids fringe; per the Army Adjutant General and Attorney General it is 'without heraldic significance', and fringe does not turn a flag into a flag of war.

commonlyWrong.text: The US government went bankrupt in 1933 and pledged citizens as collateral
commonlyWrong.note: Treasury describes the story that the government 'somehow went bankrupt' in 1933 and traded citizens' birth certificates, and calls the theory 'bogus and incomprehensible'.

commonlyWrong.text: Moorish Americans are a sovereign people exempt from US law under a treaty with Morocco
commonlyWrong.note: Seventh Circuit (Posner): the claim that eighteenth-century treaties put Moors outside US jurisdiction and taxation has no basis in fact; a self-described Moor is a US citizen with no immunity from US law, and the suit was frivolous.

commonlyWrong.text: Removing or bypassing a utility meter lets you stop paying for energy
commonlyWrong.note: Meter tampering is abstracting electricity, a crime, and the supply charges remain owed.

commonlyWrong.text: Sending police or officials a fee schedule creates a debt they must pay
commonlyWrong.note: Unilateral fee schedules create no contract; no court has enforced one and some senders have been prosecuted.

commonlyWrong.text: The Uniform Commercial Code is the source of motor vehicle licensing law
commonlyWrong.note: Maryland had a full motor vehicle licensing and registration statute in 1910, upheld in 1915 as police power, decades before the UCC existed.

commonlyWrong.text: Writing a phrase such as "under duress" next to a signature voids the legal obligation
commonlyWrong.note: Duress is a factual defence that must be proven; a notation on a signature does not create it.

claim.note: Monitoring groups documented heavy crossover since 2020, though membership counts are estimates.

priorRecord.note: Monitoring groups documented heavy crossover since 2020, though membership counts are estimates.

evidenceRecord.note: Trackers report an upsurge with Covid, with estimates rising to 500,000 in 2022 (methodology questionable), and QAnon links appear in the antipodes; MAGA recruiting is not addressed.

claim.text: The UCC rights-reservation section was renumbered from 1-207 to 1-308 to stop people using it
claim.note: The section was indeed formerly 1-207, but the official comment says it is 'identical to former Section 1-207', so the renumbering changed nothing and gives no sign of an aim to stop its use.

priorRecord.note: It moved in the 2001 revision of UCC Article 1 as part of a general renumbering, not to block users.

claim.note: Researchers who check claimed wins find none on the theory; apparent wins are dismissals on ordinary grounds or unverifiable.

evidenceRecord.note: Promised successes are 'at best, rumour' and failures go undisclosed; one guru misdescribed his acquittal, but a few real wins on ordinary grounds exist.

claim.text: Sovereign citizens misread court opinions by quoting recited facts or arguments as if they were the ruling

evidenceRecord.note: OPCA applicants often cite cases that say the opposite (McMillan) or are irrelevant, which shows misreading in general but not the specific recited-facts mechanism.

evidenceRecord.note: Litigants dodge Meads by disclaiming being OPCA litigants (and Jacobi denied being a Freeman) while advancing the same pseudolaw; no trend data.

claim.text: A person can ignore a licensing law that restricts a constitutional right and act with impunity
claim.note: Licensing does not unlawfully restrict the right to travel; the defendant who ignored it was convicted and the convictions were affirmed.

priorRecord.note: Shuttlesworth allows ignoring a facially unconstitutional, standardless speech permit, but it does not reach driver licensing.

evidenceRecord.note: Licensing does not unlawfully restrict the right to travel; the defendant who ignored it was convicted and the convictions were affirmed.

claim.text: The US sovereign-citizen movement numbers in the hundreds of thousands
claim.note: SPLC estimates around 300,000, but there is no membership and figures are rough guesses.

claim.text: The constitutional right to travel protects moving between states, not operating a vehicle
claim.note: Ohio holds the travel right does not cover driving a car, but also recognizes a fundamental right of intrastate travel, so the 'between states' limit is too narrow.

priorRecord.note: Crandall, Shapiro and Saenz concern interstate movement and residency, not vehicle operation.
